title: Booth Recoding: A Run of Ones Costs Two Operations
unit: Computer Arithmetic: Fixed and Floating Point
quickIdea: Booth reads the multiplier two bits at a time and turns a run of ones into one subtraction at its bottom and one addition at its top, so signed numbers multiply with no separate sign fix-up.
remember: Pair table, reading (q_i, q_{i-1}): 00 and 11 do nothing, 01 adds the multiplicand, 10 subtracts it.
The identity behind it: a run of ones from weight 2^m up to 2^k is 2^(k+1) - 2^m, so 001110 (14) is 16 - 2 and 0111 (7) is 8 - 1.
The state is A (accumulator), Q (multiplier) and one extra bit q(-1) holding the bit just shifted out of Q. A and q(-1) start at 0.
Every cycle ends with an arithmetic right shift of A:Q:q(-1) - the top bit of A is copied back into A's sign position, which is what keeps the partial product's value halved rather than corrupted.
It works on the two's complement patterns directly, so negative multiplicands and negative multipliers need no correction step at the end.
An n-bit multiplier takes n cycles and leaves the 2n-bit product in A:Q.

example.prompt: Multiply 11 by 14 in 5 bits with Booth's algorithm.
example.answer: A:Q = 00100 11010 = 154 = 11 x 14, from two arithmetic operations instead of the three the multiplier's ones would need.

gateAngle: The two Booth questions in this topic test the recoding's cost rather than a full trace - GATE CSE 1996 Q.1.23 asks which multiplier pattern is worst and GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.22 asks how many operations a given multiplier needs - so the pair table and the trace are the machinery behind them, and both sit on the next card.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Multiply -6 by 3 with Booth's algorithm in 4 bits: M = 1010, Q = 0011.
variations.why: Pairs of Q with q(-1) = 0, least significant first: 10, 11, 01, 00, so subtract, shift, shift, add, shift. The trace ends with A = 1110 and Q = 1110, and 1110 1110 is -18, which is (-6) x 3.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does Booth's algorithm need an arithmetic right shift rather than a logical one?
variations.answer: Because A holds a signed partial product; a logical shift would insert 0 into the sign position and change the value whenever A is negative.
variations.why: The shift is a division by two of the pair A:Q, and for a negative A only sign propagation preserves the value. Copying A's top bit into its own sign position is the whole difference.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A 16-bit Booth multiplier is given Q = 1111111111111111. How many additions or subtractions does it perform?
variations.why: With q(-1) = 0 the only differing pair is (1,0) at the least significant end; every other pair is 11. A multiplier of all ones is 2^16 - 1, which is exactly one subtraction at weight 2^0.

trap.what: Reversing the pair table - adding on 10 and subtracting on 01 - or replacing the arithmetic shift with a logical one.
trap.why: The pair is read least significant bit first: 10 marks the bottom end of a run of ones and 01 marks the top end. Swapping them negates every recoded digit, so the trace computes -M x Q.
trap.counterexample: M = 01011 (11) with Q = 01110 (14) gives 154 under the correct table and -154 under the reversed one. And with a logical shift, the cycle-2 A of 10101 would become 01010 instead of 11010, and the product would not be 154.

check.question: Recode the 6-bit multiplier 011100 with Booth. How many arithmetic operations does it need, and what are they?
check.answer: Two: one subtraction at the bottom of the run and one addition at the top.
check.explanation: Pairs, least significant first with q(-1) = 0: 00, 00, 10, 11, 11, 01, which recodes to 0, 0, -1, 0, 0, +1. And 011100 is 28 = 32 - 4, which is exactly that subtraction and addition.

The Hindi article says q(-1) is 'Qn incremented by 1' and stops after 'n-1 bits'; both readings are wrong against the standard treatment and are not used - q(-1) is the bit shifted out of Q, and the loop runs n cycles.
